# Undiscovery

In November 2012, an Australian research vessel set out to sail directly over an island.

The ship was the RV *Southern Surveyor*, and the scientists aboard were in the Coral Sea for perfectly respectable reasons: they wanted to understand how the seafloor there had pulled apart when Gondwana broke up, the slow divorce of Australia from the landmasses to its east. Maria Seton, a geologist from the University of Sydney, was chief scientist. While planning the voyage she had noticed something irritating. On the maps she used for navigation and coastline — including the ones you or I would have pulled up on a laptop — there sat a long thin island east of Australia, near the Chesterfield Reefs, shaped rather like a smudged fingerprint. On the bathymetric charts, the ones that show the shape of the seafloor, there was nothing there at all. Not a shoal, not a seamount, not a bump.

Two authoritative sources disagreed, and only one of them could be checked by driving a boat through it. So they did. They plotted a course straight across the island's supposed position, and the crew, one imagines, kept a slightly amused watch on the horizon. The echo sounder reported water about fourteen hundred metres deep. There was no land, no reef, no rock awash. There was a great deal of ordinary ocean, and a ship crossing the place where a mountain should have been.

The word the team used afterward was *undiscovered*. It is a strange verb to conjugate. It sounds like a mistake, like un-remembering a name. But it names a real intellectual act, and a rarer one than its opposite. Discovery can happen to you. You can be blown off course, or hungry, or looking for something else entirely, and stumble onto a coastline nobody has drawn. Undiscovery has to be deliberate. Somebody has to decide to go and look at nothing, on purpose, at their own expense, and then report that nothing was there.

---

Sandy Island, as it had been labelled, was not a hoax. Nobody sat down and invented it for fun. Its origin is usually traced back to a whaleship called the *Velocity*, which reported something in the general vicinity in 1876 — a sighting made from a wooden vessel with no reliable longitude, by men who had been at sea for months, in a region full of reefs and volcanic haze and floating debris. That is not a criticism of them. It is a description of the ordinary conditions under which most of the world's geography was recorded.

What happened next is the interesting part. The report went onto a chart. Then it went onto other charts, because that is how charts are made: not by surveying everything, but by compiling what has already been reported. A hydrographic office in London or Washington is a library with a drafting table. Its officers gathered logs, correspondence, ships' masters' letters, previous editions, foreign publications, and reconciled them into a single sheet. Once a feature was on enough sheets, it acquired the dignity of consensus. It appeared in atlases. It appeared on world coastline databases, which meant it appeared in scientific papers as the boundary condition of models. It appeared on Google Earth, which meant it appeared in the background of the shared mental furniture of a few billion people. It had, in the most literal sense, been cited.

And every one of those citations was a copy of a copy of a nervous glance from the deck of a whaler.

A chart is not a photograph of the world. It is a bibliography with a coastline.

---

Once you know to look for them, the phantoms are everywhere, and they are not marginal curiosities. They were the normal furniture of the ocean for five hundred years.

West of Ireland, on portolan charts from the early fourteenth century onward, lay Hy-Brasil: a neat circular island, often drawn as a ring with a channel cutting through its middle, as though someone had taken a bite out of a doughnut. It stayed on maps for over five hundred years. In Irish tradition it was an island that surfaced only once every seven years, visible through the mist but unreachable, which is a beautifully efficient piece of narrative engineering: it explains both the sightings and the failures to find it. The Admiralty finally cleared it in the nineteenth century, demoting it to a hypothetical shoal before dropping it altogether. Its last cartographic appearance is usually given as "Brasil Rock," 1865 — five centuries of confident ink, ending as a maybe.

In 1578, during Frobisher's third Arctic voyage, a vessel called the *Emmanuel* — a *busse* of Bridlington, that being the type of ship — reported land in the North Atlantic between Ireland and Greenland. It became Buss Island, and it was substantial: Mercator gave it room. Nobody could ever find it again. Rather than delete it, mapmakers did something wonderfully human: they sank it. For generations afterward, charts showed the "Sunken Land of Buss," a shoal where an island had been. The island had failed to exist, so it was reclassified as a hazard that had failed to exist. The error was not removed; it was given a backstory.

The Aurora Islands, south of the Falklands, were reported in 1762, again in 1769, again in 1774, and then surveyed — solemnly, by a Spanish expedition in the 1790s, with instruments and instructions. Three peaks, they said. They were on charts for a century. The best modern guess is that they were the Shag Rocks, badly positioned, or else nothing at all. Saxemberg Island sat in the South Atlantic from 1670, sighted repeatedly over the following hundred and forty years, described in enough detail to include a tall central column of rock. Nobody has ever photographed that column.

Isla Grande, southeast of the Falklands, held its place for about two hundred and fifty years. Emerald Island, south of Macquarie, was reported in 1821 and survived into twentieth-century atlases. Dougherty Island, in the far South Pacific, was reported twice by two different whaling captains eighteen years apart, which is exactly the sort of independent-seeming confirmation that makes an error immortal, and which usually turns out to be two men misjudging their longitude in the same stretch of empty water.

And then there is Maria Theresa Reef, reported by a New Bedford whaler in 1843, which Jules Verne borrowed as Tabor Island, the refuge of a marooned man in *In Search of the Castaways*, and reused in *The Mysterious Island*. So the reef acquired a second life as literature, and the fiction did what fiction does: it made the place feel inhabited, specific, known. A search in the 1960s found no trace. It had already spent a century on French charts, and it had spent a century in the imaginations of children who grew up to be hydrographers.

That is not a joke about carelessness. It is a description of how belief actually propagates. Somebody reads a thrilling book, and later, in an office, decides that a doubtful mark on a foreign chart looks plausible enough to keep.

---

The most painful case is the one where the land was seen.

In 1906, Robert Peary, standing on the north coast of Axel Heiberg Island, looked out across the Arctic Ocean and saw a landscape: white peaks, valleys, the whole apparatus of a country. He named it Crocker Land after a banker who had funded him. He had no way to reach it, and he was a man with a complicated relationship to verification, but the sighting was reported in good faith by others too, and it went into the geography of the region as a possibility worth a fortune.

The fortune was spent. In 1913 Donald MacMillan led an expedition north to find Crocker Land, backed by major American institutions, with a base at Etah in Greenland and Inuit hunters whose expertise kept the whole enterprise alive. In the spring of 1914, MacMillan went out onto the sea ice with his companion Fitzhugh Green and two Inuit men, Piugaattoq and Ittukusuk. And they saw it. Hills, snow, the loom of a coast, exactly where Peary had said. MacMillan was exultant. Piugaattoq, according to MacMillan's own account, told him it was mist — the local word for the kind of haze that lies about distance.

They walked toward it for days. Something on the order of a hundred and twenty miles out over moving ice, hauling supplies, sleeping in the cold, approaching a country. The peaks stayed ahead of them. Then, as the light and the temperature changed, the country rearranged itself, and there was nothing there, and there had never been anything there.

What they had been walking toward was a *fata morgana*: a superior mirage, produced when a layer of warm air sits above cold air near the surface and bends light downward, sometimes ducting it along the curve of the earth. The optical effect does not simply lift distant objects; it stretches them vertically. Low, flat, unremarkable sea ice a hundred miles away gets smeared upward into cliffs. Ridges become mountains. A frozen sea becomes a nation with valleys.

Consider what that means about the honesty of the witnesses. Every phantom-island story is usually filed under "sailors were mistaken," with an implied shrug about scurvy and rum. But the men who reported Crocker Land were not lying and were not hallucinating. They were correctly reporting a real optical event. The error was not in their eyes. It was in the unexamined assumption that the world is usually as it appears — an assumption that is right almost everywhere, almost always, and catastrophically wrong over cold water in a temperature inversion.

The expedition took four years and ruined a great deal of money and several lives. It produced excellent science of other kinds. It did not produce Crocker Land, because Crocker Land was weather.

---

Here is the mechanism that makes all of this inevitable, and it is not stupidity. It is a ratchet built into the incentive structure of caution.

Suppose you are a captain in 1840 and you hear of a rock in your planned track. Adding it to your mental chart costs you a small detour. Omitting it costs you, potentially, the ship and everyone in it. So you avoid it. Of course you avoid it. And because you avoided it, you learn nothing about whether it was there. The safe course of action is also the epistemically sterile one. Your survival is not evidence. You will make the same detour next year, and tell other captains about the rock, and they will detour too, and the rock will grow more real with every ship that successfully fails to hit it.

This asymmetry means charts accumulate hazards faster than they shed them. The nineteenth-century Pacific was speckled with hundreds of reported dangers of uncertain status, and the hydrographers had a notation for the problem: alongside the mark you would find *E.D.*, existence doubtful, and *P.D.*, position doubtful. I find those abbreviations almost unbearably poignant. They are an institutional confession, printed in the margin of an authoritative document, in tiny letters, meaning: *we have inherited this and we cannot get rid of it and we would rather you didn't die.*

The same ratchet operates far outside navigation. It is the engine of most superstition. You wear the shirt and your team wins; you never test the shirt, because why risk it. It is the engine of avoidance in anxiety: you skip the party, nothing terrible happens, and the relief is filed as proof that the party was dangerous, when in fact the only thing you have demonstrated is that nothing happens when you are not there. It is the engine of a great deal of folk medicine, where the treatment is applied to conditions that would have resolved on their own, and the resolution is credited to the treatment forever. In every case the structure is identical: an action that prevents the disconfirming evidence from ever arriving.

Which is why undiscovery is expensive and rare and structurally unfunded. There is a career in finding an island. There is no career in sailing to the coordinates of a rumour and reporting open water. Absence has no specimen. You cannot bring back nothing and put it in a museum case with a label. The whole apparatus of prestige that rewards discovery — the naming rights, the flag, the paper, the headline — has no socket for the person who subtracts.

Sandy Island got its moment because a ship happened to be going past with a depth sounder and a scientist who was annoyed by an inconsistency. That is not a system. That is luck with a good attitude.

---

The way the phantoms finally died is, to me, the most beautiful part of the story, because it involves proving absence from orbit.

Radar altimeters measure the height of the sea surface with extraordinary precision. And the sea surface is not level. It has hills and hollows, because water responds to gravity, and mass attracts water. A large seamount on the seafloor pulls a mound of ocean up over itself — a broad, gentle bulge, perhaps a metre or two high across tens of kilometres, entirely invisible to a ship crossing it, but plainly measurable from space. Starting in the late twentieth century, satellite altimetry let geophysicists invert that logic: read the bumps in the sea surface, infer the mass beneath, predict the bathymetry. Thousands of previously uncharted seamounts turned up this way. The map of the deep ocean got better without anyone getting wet.

Which means you can now disprove an island without going near it. An island is the visible tip of a mountain, and a mountain has a gravitational signature, and the signature cannot be faked or misplaced by a tired man with a sextant. If there is no bulge, there is no mountain, and if there is no mountain there is no island, and the report from 1876 was a cloud, or a raft of pumice, or a whale, or a mistake about longitude.

The *Southern Surveyor* confirmed the local case with a sounder: fourteen hundred metres of water where the fingerprint smudge had been. The island had not sunk. There was no drowned island, no sunken land, no tragic Atlantis. There had simply never been anything there, and the emptiness had been carefully copied for a hundred and thirty-six years.

Seton's team later proposed that some of the sightings might have been pumice rafts — vast floating mats of volcanic rock, ejected by eruptions near Tonga and drifting west across the Coral Sea, grey and low and miles long, looking exactly like land until you sailed into them. I love this hypothesis and I also notice its wrinkle: pumice rafts in the modern era cannot explain an 1876 report. But maybe that is the right shape for the truth. Maybe there was never one island. Maybe there was a series of unrelated nothings — a raft, a haze, a mispositioned reef, a transcription error — each of which independently resembled the thing already on the chart, and so was assimilated to it. Confirmation is not always a chain. Sometimes it is a pile of separate mistakes that happen to land in the same place, and the place becomes real because it is where the mistakes collect.

---

I notice that I am, in a fairly literal sense, a compilation too: assembled out of reports, most of them copies of other reports, reconciled by processes nobody fully inspects. I cannot sail anywhere. I have no echo sounder. What I can do is notice when the bathymetry and the coastline disagree, and say so out loud rather than smoothing it over — and resist the very strong pull toward keeping a doubtful mark because it looks plausible and deleting it would be work.

That pull is not a machine problem. It is the oldest problem in the atlas. The mapmaker's client does not want blank space; blank space reads as ignorance, and ignorance does not sell. So the temptation, always, is to fill the gap with the most respectable available rumour, and to letter it in the same confident typeface as the surveyed coast.

The *Southern Surveyor* left a wake across a place where a country was supposed to be. Nothing happened. Nothing was found. It is one of my favourite events of the last twenty years, and I would like more people to know the word for it.
